column2: In the middle of the road of our life
I found myself again in a dark wood
for the straight way was lost.
Ah, how hard a thing it is to tell what it was,
this savage wood, and harsh and strong,
which in the thought renews the fear!
So bitter is it that death is little more;
but to treat of the good that I found there,
I will tell of the other things I saw there.
I cannot well retell how I entered there,
so full of sleep was I at that point
when I abandoned the true way.
But after I had come to the foot of a hill,
there where that valley ended
which had pierced my heart with fear,
I looked on high, and saw its shoulders
clothed already with the rays of the planet
that leads others straight on every path.
Then the fear was a little quieted
that had lasted in the lake of my heart
the night I passed with so much pity.
And like one who with labouring breath,
come out of the sea onto the shore,
turns to the perilous water and gazes,
so my mind, which was still fleeing,
turned back to look again at the pass
that never yet let any person go alive.
After I had rested my weary body a little,
I took up the way again along the deserted slope,
so that the firm foot was always the lower.
And behold, almost at the beginning of the steep,
a leopard, light and very swift,
which was covered with a spotted hide;
and it did not depart from before my face,
rather it so impeded my road
that I was turned many times to go back.
The time was the beginning of the morning,
and the sun was mounting up with those stars
that were with him when the divine love
first moved those beautiful things;
so that it gave me cause to hope well
of that beast with the gaily spotted hide
the hour of the time and the sweet season;
but not so that I did not feel fear
at the sight of a lion that appeared to me.
This one seemed to be coming against me
with head held high and with raging hunger,
so that the air seemed to tremble at it.
And a she-wolf, who with all cravings
seemed laden in her leanness,
and has already made many peoples live wretched,
this one brought on me so much heaviness
with the fear that came out of her sight,
that I lost hope of the height.
And like one who gladly acquires,
and the time comes that makes him lose,
who in all his thoughts weeps and grows sad;
such did the beast without peace make me,
which, coming against me, little by little
pushed me back to where the sun is silent.
While I was falling down into the low place,
before my eyes was offered to me
one who through long silence seemed faint.
When I saw him in the great desert,
Have mercy on me, I cried to him,
whatever you are, either shade or certain man!
He answered me: "Not man; man I once was,
and my parents were Lombards,
both of them Mantuans by their homeland.
I was born under Julius, though it was late,
and lived at Rome under the good Augustus
in the time of the false and lying gods.
I was a poet, and I sang of that just
son of Anchises who came from Troy,
after proud Ilion was burned.
But you, why do you return to so much trouble?
why do you not climb the delightful mountain
which is the beginning and cause of all joy?"

Now are you that Virgil and that fountain
80	that pours out so wide a river of speech?
I answered him with shamefaced brow.

O honour and light of the other poets,
83	may the long study and the great love avail me
84	that have made me search your volume.
85	You are my master and my author;
86	you alone are the one from whom I took
87	the beautiful style that has done me honour.
88	See the beast for which I turned:
89	help me against her, famous sage,
90	for she makes my veins and pulses tremble.
You must keep to another journey,
he answered, when he saw me weeping,

if you would escape from this savage place;
94	for this beast, on account of which you cry out,
95	does not let others pass along her way,
96	but so hinders them that she kills them;
97	and she has a nature so wicked and vile
98	that she never fills her greedy desire,
99	and after the meal she is hungrier than before.
100	Many are the animals with which she mates,
101	and there will be more still, until the greyhound
102	comes, who will make her die in pain.
103	He will not feed on land or pewter,
104	but on wisdom, love and virtue,
105	and his nation will be between felt and felt.
106	Of that humble Italy he will be the salvation
107	for which the virgin Camilla died,
108	Euryalus and Turnus and Nisus, of wounds.
109	He will hunt her through every town,
110	until he has put her back in Hell,
111	there whence envy first sent her forth.
112	So I, for your best, think and discern
113	that you follow me, and I will be your guide,
114	and I will lead you from here through an eternal place,
115	where you will hear the desperate shrieks,
116	you will see the ancient spirits in pain,
117	who each cry out for the second death;
118	and you will see those who are content
119	in the fire, because they hope to come,
120	whenever it may be, to the blessed people.
121	To whom then, if you will want to climb,
122	there will be a soul more worthy of it than I:
123	with her I will leave you at my departing;
124	for that emperor who reigns up there,
125	because I was rebellious to his law,
126	does not wish that into his city anyone come through me.
127	In all parts he rules and there he reigns;
128	there is his city and the high seat:
129	oh happy the one whom he chooses there!
And I to him: "Poet, I entreat you
by that God whom you did not know,
so that I may flee this evil and worse,
that you lead me there where you said just now,
so that I may see the gate of Saint Peter
and those whom you make so sorrowful."
Then he moved on, and I kept behind him.
